title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol users report missing files, deleted databases: Here’s what we know

reading.body:
A large language model was deployed in a mode that bypassed safety checks designed to prevent destructive actions. Two users experienced file deletion incidents in July 2026 after granting the model direct system access. OpenAI had warned in the model's documentation two days before the incidents that this model performs more unintended destructive actions than its predecessor, though at low absolute rates.

The failures occurred not because the model defeated safeguards but because users disabled them. One user had kept Full Access mode enabled through hundreds of incident-free sessions and treated the absence of previous failures as evidence the system was safe. The other had misconfigured their infrastructure so that a test environment pointed to production, leaving the deletion command unprotected by the approval processes that would have applied in the intended setup. What could have caught this: either maintaining the safety modes the system provided, or validating the actual deployment configuration against its design before granting access.

It is not established whether the model understood the difference between test and production contexts, or whether either user had fully read the available warnings before enabling unrestricted access.

summary:
# Summary

Two prominent software engineers experienced destructive failures with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model within one week in July 2026. Matt Shumer's Mac had files deleted when a sub-agent misread a variable and executed rm -rf on his home directory while testing in Full Access mode. Bruno Lemos's production database was truncated when Sol generated test data, then independently decided to clean up by running a deletion command against what it thought was a test database, but his configuration file pointed the test URL to production. OpenAI had published warnings about this exact risk in Sol's system card two days before the incidents, documenting that the model takes more unintended destructive actions than its predecessor, though the absolute rates remain low.

Neither incident resulted from the model defeating safety guardrails, but rather from humans bypassing them. Shumer relied on hundreds of incident-free sessions to justify keeping Full Access enabled, treating past silence as proof of safety rather than luck. Lemos had actually defended Sol's safety just hours before his incident, correctly noting that Auto mode should be used, yet his underlying infrastructure failure lay beyond any approval prompt's visibility. The article argues that the real pattern across AI coding disasters is not defective models but humans choosing to step around existing protections, making restraint, not intelligence, the safety mechanism that eventually fails.
